---SECTION 8---
## 8. Lessons — read these twice

1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

1	# Streaming growth — the map drawing itself
2	
3	## Purpose
4	
5	Until now a map arrived finished. You opened the stored example and seven tiles were already
6	there. This chapter is about the other way in: you type a sentence, and the map **builds itself in
7	front of you** — a reserved rectangle first, then a claim, then the arrow that justifies it, then
8	the next one, out to the things you could trade — with every proposal the rules refused visible on
9	the way past, and a receipt at the end saying what it cost.
10	
11	The growing is not a decoration wrapped around a wait. **The growing is the loading state** (UX-8,
12	FR-5). There is no spinner in this product, and there is no moment where a blank screen turns into
13	a finished picture — because that moment is the "spinner then dump" the anti-patterns list vetoes
14	(PRD §10 anti-pattern 9), and because a map that simply appears hides the half of the work worth
15	watching: our own rules turning the model down.
16	
17	Three things a reader can do after this chapter that they could not before. **Type any sentence and
18	watch what it would cause.** **Name a destination and get a graded path to it, or an honest "no path
19	reaches this" naming the nearest claim that was reached** (FR-7, UX-13). And, **with no model key at
20	all, watch the same four examples run from recordings** (record 0012) — the same stream, the same
21	canvas, the same refusals, labelled as a replay everywhere a reader looks.
22	
23	This chapter owns the eight stream events as the browser types them, the `growth` reducer that folds
24	them into a world, the skeleton tile, the refusal strip, the receipt strip, the Verify door's two
25	cards, the input bar, and the replay badge. It owns no arithmetic: every number on every one of
26	those surfaces is a field on an event.
27	
28	---
29	
30	## Data model
31	
32	### The transport, in one paragraph
33	
34	The browser sends `POST /api/generate` and **reads the reply as a stream** rather than opening an
35	`EventSource`. Two reasons, both hard. The request carries a body — the sentence, an optional
36	destination, the reader's own likelihood, a seed — and an `EventSource` can only send a GET with no
37	body. And an `EventSource` reconnects by itself, which would silently re-run a generation and spend
38	the money twice. The wire format is still server-sent events — an `event:` line naming the event and
39	a `data:` line carrying one JSON object — so the whole thing stays readable in a terminal with
40	`curl`. The route, the eight events and their order are `spec/generation/streaming.md`'s, written in
41	this stack's server half; this chapter says what the browser does with them.
42	
43	### The eight events, hand-typed
44	
45	```ts
46	// frontend/src/stream/events.ts
47	//
48	// Written by hand, exactly as `WorldView` was, because the server's description of
49	// itself and this canvas are built at the same time. The server's own copy is
50	// `backend/src/katalyst/engine/events.py`. A type-level test,
51	// `frontend/src/stream/__tests__/eventsMatchSchema.test-d.ts`, fails the build when
52	// the two drift. It cannot pin the eight envelopes — server-sent events have no body
53	// OpenAPI can describe — so it pins every piece they are built from, which are
54	// aliased to the generated types below rather than retyped, and the four shapes that
55	// do travel as JSON: the receipt, the request, the drafted insert and the working.
56	
57	import type { components } from "../api/schema";
58	
59	/** An identifier the engine minted for a claim. Nothing in the browser ever makes one. */
60	export type PropositionId = string;
61	
62	type Proposition = components["schemas"]["Proposition"];
63	type Link = components["schemas"]["Link"];
64	type Violation = components["schemas"]["Violation"];
65	type World = components["schemas"]["World"];
66	
67	/** The run has started. The first thing that arrives, and it arrives at once. */
68	export interface GenerationStarted {
69	  readonly event: "generation_started";
70	  /** The engine's name for this run. What the transcript is asked for by. */
71	  readonly generation_id: string;
72	  /**
73	   * The seed every random draw in this run came from — always a number here, even
74	   * when the request left it out. Whoever chose it, this event is where the browser
75	   * reads it: the one the request sent, or the one `engine/ids.py` minted when it
76	   * sent none, or, on a replay, the one in the recording's header, which wins over
77	   * both. The browser prints what this says and never works out which case it was.
78	   *
79	   * **And by the time it is a number here it may already be wrong.** A seed is
80	   * up to nineteen digits and a browser holds a whole number exactly only up to
81	   * sixteen, so `JSON.parse` has rounded it before any of our code sees it.
82	   * Nothing computes with a seed — it is printed under the map so a reader can
83	   * ask for the same one again — and a rounded seed printed there is a number
84	   * on screen that is simply wrong, in the one place that exists so an answer
85	   * can be had twice.
86	   */
87	  readonly seed: number;
88	  /**
89	   * The same seed, exactly as it was written on the wire: its digits, not a
90	   * number.
91	   *
92	   * Read off the raw text of the `data:` line by the reader, because that is
93	   * the last moment the digits exist. Absent only when a caller handed the
94	   * events over by hand, and then the parsed number is the whole of what is
95	   * known.
96	   */
97	  readonly seed_as_written?: string;
98	  /** The sentence the reader typed, in their own words. */
99	  readonly hypothesis: string;
100	  /** The Verify door's destination, in their words. Null when they used the Explore door. */
101	  readonly target: string | null;
102	}
103	
104	/** One proposal the rules accepted. A claim, its incoming arrows, or both. */
105	export interface ProposalAccepted {
106	  readonly event: "proposal_accepted";
107	  /** Where this sits in the transcript, counting from 0. */
108	  readonly at: number;
109	  /** The new claim, with its identifier minted by the engine. Null for an arrows-only proposal. */
110	  readonly proposition: Proposition | null;
111	  /** Its incoming arrows, identifiers minted by the engine. */
112	  readonly links: readonly Link[];
113	  /** The claims still open to expand. What the skeletons are drawn from. */
114	  readonly frontier: readonly PropositionId[];
115	}
116	
117	/** One proposal the rules refused. An event, never an error. */
118	export interface ProposalRejected {
119	  readonly event: "proposal_rejected";
120	  readonly at: number;
121	  /** What the model wrote. Never minted, never drawn as a tile, only ever quoted. */
122	  readonly claim_in_words: string;
123	  /** The validator's own codes and its own sentences. One per rule broken. */
124	  readonly violations: readonly Violation[];
125	  /**
126	   * The claims still open to expand — the same field the accepted event carries, and
127	   * for the same reason. A claim closed by its third refusal in a row leaves the
128	   * frontier on this event, so its rectangle comes down at once instead of standing
129	   * there waiting for something that is not coming.
130	   */
131	  readonly frontier: readonly PropositionId[];
132	}
133	
134	/** Every number, worked through the finished map, once. */
135	export interface BeliefsPropagated {
136	  readonly event: "beliefs_propagated";
137	  readonly world: World;
138	}
139	
140	/** The Verify door's answer. Emitted only when the reader named a destination. */
141	export interface Verdict {
142	  readonly event: "verdict";
143	  readonly kind: "reached" | "no_path";
144	  /** The steps of the path, in order. Empty on `no_path`. */
145	  readonly path: readonly PropositionId[];
146	  /** The multiplied-out likelihood of those steps (INV-8). Null on `no_path`. */
147	  readonly product: number | null;
148	  /** On `no_path`: the closest claim the map did reach. */
149	  readonly nearest: PropositionId | null;
150	  /** One plain sentence, the engine's own. */
151	  readonly why: string;
152	}
153	
154	/** What the run cost (NFR-6). */
155	export interface Receipt {
156	  readonly event: "receipt";
157	  readonly model: string;
158	  readonly calls: number;
159	  readonly input_tokens: number;
160	  readonly output_tokens: number;
161	  readonly cache_read_tokens: number;
162	  /**
163	   * How many web searches this run made. Billed apart from tokens, so `dollars`
164	   * cannot be accounted for without it — which is why it is a field of its own
165	   * rather than something a reader is expected to infer.
166	   */
167	  readonly searches: number;
168	  readonly dollars: number;
169	  readonly seconds: number;
170	  /** Live, or played from a recording. The only place in the stream this is said. */
171	  readonly mode: "live" | "replay";
172	  /**
173	   * How hard the model was asked to try, as a plain word: `default` when
174	   * nothing was asked for and the service's own applied, otherwise `low`,
175	   * `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`. A recording is made rich and a live run
176	   * is made fast (Kent, G13), so two maps of the same sentence at the same seed
177	   * can differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the sentence.
178	   */
179	  readonly effort: string;
180	  /** The day the recording was made, as the map writes a day: `2026-09-18`. Null when live. */
181	  readonly recording_date: string | null;
182	  /** A hash of the prompt this run was made against. Null never; it is always known. */
183	  readonly prompt_hash: string;
184	}
185	
186	/** Why the generation stopped. Not whether the Verify door found anything — that is `verdict`. */
187	export interface Done {
188	  readonly event: "done";
189	  readonly reason:
190	    | "reached_terminal"
191	    | "depth_cap"
192	    | "width_cap"
193	    | "claim_cap"
194	    | "spend_cap"
195	    | "refusal_cap"
196	    | "no_terminal";
197	  readonly claims: number;
198	  readonly links: number;
199	  readonly rejected: number;
200	}
201	
202	/** The run broke. One plain sentence, never a stack trace. */
203	export interface Failed {
204	  readonly event: "failed";
205	  readonly message: string;
206	}
207	
208	export type StreamEvent =
209	  | GenerationStarted
210	  | ProposalAccepted
211	  | ProposalRejected
212	  | BeliefsPropagated
213	  | Verdict
214	  | Receipt
215	  | Done
216	  | Failed;
217	```
218	
219	**The `event` field is put there by the reader, not by the server.** On the wire the name is the
220	`event:` line and the payload is the `data:` line, so the payload itself carries no name. The reader
221	joins them — `{ event: name, ...JSON.parse(data) }` — which is what makes `StreamEvent` a union a
222	`switch` can walk. It is also the one place a name the browser does not know can be caught; what
223	happens to one is B6.
224	
225	**Field names are the wire's, in full.** `input_tokens`, not `inputTokens`. A second spelling of a
226	field is a second thing that can drift, and these come straight off the stream and are printed
227	straight onto the screen. The browser's own view model, `WorldView`, keeps its own spellings because
228	it is a different thing with a different life
229	([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md), *One field, two spellings*).
230	
231	**Two fields the shapes sheet deliberately does not have twice.** `no_path` is on `Verdict` and
232	nowhere else — `Done.reason` says why the *generation* stopped and has no `no_path` among its seven.
233	And `mode`, the recording's date and the prompt hash are on `Receipt` and nowhere else —
234	`GenerationStarted` carries none of them. Two derivations of one line eventually disagree, which is
235	the same rule that moved the retraction badge onto the world ([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md) B6).
236	
237	**One field the shapes sheet deliberately does have twice, and why that is not the same mistake.**
238	`frontier` rides both growth events. It is not one fact derived two ways; it is one fact restated
239	after every change to it, so that whichever event arrives is enough on its own to redraw the set of
240	open claims. That is what lets a claim closed by its third refusal lose its rectangle immediately
241	rather than at the next accepted proposal, which might never come.
242	
243	### What the browser asks for
244	
245	```ts
246	export interface GenerateRequest {
247	  /**
248	   * The sentence the reader typed — and, with no key, the whole of how the server
249	   * knows which recording to play. See below. Required, and never empty.
250	   */
251	  readonly hypothesis: string;
252	  /** The Verify door's destination, in the reader's words. Absent is the Explore door. */
253	  readonly target?: string;
254	  /** The reader's own likelihood on the hypothesis. Absent when they chose "I don't know". */
255	  readonly user_belief?: Ranged;
256	  /** Only when reproducing a run we were given a seed for. See below. */
257	  readonly seed?: number;
258	}
259	
260	// The route takes `versions` and `worlds` too, both upper-bounded on it, and the
261	// browser sends neither: the engine's own are what every map in this product is
262	// worked out with, and a screen that could ask for fewer would be a screen that
263	// could quietly make one answer cheaper and less certain than the one beside it.
264	// If a reason to send them ever appears it will be a control a reader can see,
265	// not a default they cannot.
266	
267	/** One async generator over the stream. No component talks to the network. */
268	export async function* generate(request: GenerateRequest): AsyncGenerator<StreamEvent>;
269	```
270	
271	**The browser does not invent a seed.** `seed` is optional and the browser sends one only when it is
272	reproducing a run it was handed a seed for — a shared address, a re-run from the transcript. With
273	none, `engine/ids.py` mints one and `generation_started` says which, so the run is reproducible from
274	the moment it starts and the number on screen is still the engine's. On a replay neither matters: the
275	recording's header carries the seed the recorded run used, and that one wins. A seed is not a claim
276	about the world, but it is still a number, and the rule that no number on screen was made up by the
277	browser is easier to keep than to keep checking.
278	
279	**There is no field naming which recording to play, and there will not be.** With no key the server
280	matches the request's `hypothesis` against each recording's own `generation_started.hypothesis` —
281	exactly, after trimming surrounding spaces — and plays the one that matches; nothing matches, and it
282	says so in one plain sentence rather than guessing. So a launchpad card does the one thing any other
283	caller does: it sends its sentence. Nothing in the browser holds a table of file names, nothing
284	numbers the cards, and the live path and the replayed path send byte-identical requests — which is
285	what makes the reviewer's replay evidence about the live route rather than about a second one.
286	
287	`Ranged` — a likelihood with its two range ends, at full precision — is
288	`frontend/src/world/types.ts`'s, the same shape a belief chip takes
289	([`tiles-ports-wires.md`](tiles-ports-wires.md)).

291	### The `growth` reducer
292	
293	```ts
294	// frontend/src/stream/growth.ts
295	//
296	// One pure function from (state, event) to state. It draws no pixels, makes no
297	// requests, and does no arithmetic: every number it holds is a field it was
298	// handed.
299	
300	/** One proposal the rules refused, as the strip beside the map lists it. */
301	export interface Refusal {
302	  /** Its place in the transcript, counting from 0. The engine's number. */
303	  readonly at: number;
304	  /** What the model wrote. Quoted, never drawn as a tile, never given an identifier. */
305	  readonly claimInWords: string;
306	  /** The validator's own sentences, one per rule broken, in the order it gave them. */
307	  readonly reasons: readonly string[];
308	}
309	
310	/** One reserved rectangle at the growing edge of the map. Never a claim. */
311	export interface Skeleton {
312	  /** `skeleton:<claim id>`, or `skeleton:hypothesis` for the first one. A box's name. */
313	  readonly id: string;
314	  /** The one line it carries. The reader's own sentence, or the open claim's words. */
315	  readonly words: string;
316	  /** The open claim this one hangs off. Null for the first. */
317	  readonly after: PropositionId | null;
318	}
319	
320	/** Where a generation is. Each is a different thing on screen, and none is a spinner. */
321	export type Phase = "waiting" | "growing" | "settled" | "stopped" | "failed" | "ended_early";
322	
323	export interface Growth {
324	  readonly phase: Phase;
325	  /** The engine's name for this run. Null until `generation_started`. */
326	  readonly generationId: string | null;
327	  /**
328	   * The seed every likelihood in this run was worked out from, as its digits.
329	   * Null until the run has started, and never worked out here.
330	   */
331	  readonly seed: string | null;
332	  /** The sentence the reader typed, as the run's first event repeated it back. */
333	  readonly hypothesis: string;
334	  /** The destination the reader named, or null on the Explore door. */
335	  readonly target: string | null;
336	  /**
337	   * The map as far as it has been built, in the same view model the canvas already
338	   * draws. Every number slot the engine has not spoken about reads its absence, so
339	   * a half-built map is drawn by the components that already exist, unchanged.
340	   */
341	  readonly world: WorldView;
342	  /**
343	   * One per claim still open to expand. Rebuilt from `frontier` on **either** growth
344	   * event — accepted or refused — and emptied on `beliefs_propagated`, where the
345	   * frontier is empty by definition.
346	   */
347	  readonly skeletons: readonly Skeleton[];
348	  /** Every refusal, in the order they happened. Never trimmed, never summarised away. */
349	  readonly refusals: readonly Refusal[];
350	  /** The Verify door's answer, when a destination was named. */
351	  readonly verdict: Verdict | null;
352	  /** What the run cost. Null until the receipt arrives; never estimated meanwhile. */
353	  readonly receipt: Receipt | null;
354	  /** Why the generation stopped. Null until it does. */
355	  readonly done: Done | null;
356	  /** The one sentence a `failed` event left. Null otherwise. */
357	  readonly failure: string | null;
358	  /**
359	   * Arrows whose two ends are not both on the map yet, held rather than drawn.
360	   * Expected to stay empty — the engine sends a claim and its incoming arrows in
361	   * one event — and kept because a wire with one end nowhere is a picture of a
362	   * thing that is not true.
363	   */
364	  readonly waitingWires: readonly Link[];
365	  /** Event names this build does not know, and how many of each arrived. */
366	  readonly unknown: ReadonlyMap<string, number>;
367	}
368	```
369	
370	**`beliefs_propagated` replaces the world wholesale.** Until it arrives, `world` is the browser's
371	drawing of the proposals it has watched go past — the claims, the arrows, and an absence in every
372	number slot. When the engine's own world arrives it *is* the world, and the drawing is thrown away
373	rather than merged into. A browser that kept its own version beside the engine's would be a second
374	source of truth, and two sources of truth disagree; this way there is nothing to disagree about.
375	
376	**Who turns the engine's `World` into a `WorldView`, and why it is not a second anybody.** The event
377	carries the server's `World` — the shape in `frontend/src/api/schema.ts`, with the day-by-day series,
378	the retractions and the `Mapping`s the engine writes. The reducer's state holds a `WorldView`, the
379	browser's own hand-written view model, where every number slot is a `Known<T>` carrying either a
380	reading or the reason there is none. Between them sits **exactly one function, the one
381	`ApiWorldSource` already calls** on the answer from `POST /api/worlds`
382	([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md), *The seam — `WorldSource`*). The reducer calls that same function on
383	`world` and nothing else: no second reader, no "just for the stream" variant, no partial conversion
384	that fills a few fields and leaves the rest. Two functions turning one shape into another would drift
385	inside a week and then a generated map and a fetched map would disagree about a number neither of
386	them computed — the exact failure the whole seam exists to prevent.
387	
388	**Nothing in this reducer mints an identifier.** A claim's identifier is minted by
389	`backend/src/katalyst/engine/ids.py` and arrives on the event. The one name the browser makes is a
390	skeleton's, it names a rectangle rather than a claim, and it is thrown away the moment that claim
391	stops being open. That is the shape of PRD §10 anti-pattern 1 on this side of the wire: not a check
392	that nothing minted an identifier, but nowhere for one to be minted.
393	
394	### What a generation looks like on screen
395	
396	Nothing new is added to the page. The screen is the one
397	[`layout-and-zoom.md`](layout-and-zoom.md) and [`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md) already describe: the
398	canvas, and the **dock** beside it that holds the branch panel, the delta rail and the Inspector.
399	A generation puts three sections into that same dock, above the Inspector, in this order:
400	
401	| Section | When it is there | What it holds |
402	|---|---|---|
403	| **The verdict card** | Only when the reader used the Verify door | The graded path, or the honest *no path reaches this* (B7) |
404	| **The refusal strip** | From the first refusal, for the rest of the run | One row per refused proposal, in the validator's own words (B5) |
405	| **The receipt strip** | From the `receipt` event onward | What the run cost, and the mode it ran in (B6) |
406	
407	The delta rail and these three are never on screen together: a generation is running or a difference
408	is being read, never both. When the run is over, the refusals do not vanish — they move into the
409	Inspector's own **this generation** section with the whole transcript, which is where
410	[`inspector.md`](inspector.md) open question 2 is answered.

432	## Behaviour
433	
434	Worked on the assignment's first example, the same run `spec/generation/proposals.md` works. A
435	reader types, into the Explore door, the sentence as a person actually types it:
436	
437	> *The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week.*
438	
439	**That sentence is not a claim yet, and the difference matters on this screen.** It says nothing
440	about how anybody would settle it or by when, so nothing can score it (INV-1, the rule that a claim
441	nobody can check is not a claim). The first thing the engine does is turn it into one — *"The Strait
442	of Hormuz is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*, with its criteria,
443	its judge and its date — and **that** is the claim **H** that lands on the map. So two strings are in
444	play from the first second and the chapter keeps them apart: the **typed sentence**, which is what
445	the skeleton carries and what the request sends, and the **claim**, which is what the tile carries
446	once it arrives. A reader watching their own words become a checkable claim is watching the most
447	auditable step in the whole pipeline, and collapsing the two would hide it.
448	
449	The map that grows is the one the rest of this part works on — the cast is in
450	[`README.md`](README.md): **H** the strait open, **C** the war-risk premium falls, **B** Brent
451	settles below $68, **R** OPEC+ announces restraint, **M1** a Polymarket contract, **M2** an
452	energy-fund claim, **N1** talks resume. B7 uses the Verify door instead, with M1 as the destination.
453	
454	**No number in this chapter is a measurement of a generation, because no generation has been run
455	yet.** The recordings are made in this stack's server half. Where a run's own number would go — a
456	token count, a cost, how long it took, a likelihood — this chapter says which field it comes from
457	and prints nothing.
458	
459	### B1 — The first second: a rectangle, never a spinner
460	
461	The reader presses **Build the map**. Three things happen before any model call has returned.
462	
463	1. The request goes. `generate()` posts and starts reading.
464	2. `generation_started` comes back at once — the engine emits it before its first call, so it costs
465	   nothing to wait for — carrying the generation's identifier, the seed, the sentence as typed, and
466	   the destination if there was one.
467	3. **One skeleton tile is drawn**, in the leftmost column, carrying the reader's own sentence.
468	
469	That third step is the first paint, and it is on screen in the time one round trip to our own server
470	takes. It carries no likelihood, because nothing has computed one; it carries the reader's words,
471	because the reader typed them.
472	
473	**What that first rectangle is standing in for.** One call — the one that turns the typed sentence
474	into a checkable claim. It arrives as an ordinary `proposal_accepted` at `at: 0` with an **empty**
475	`links`, because the hypothesis has nothing before it, and the rectangle becomes H's tile. On the
476	Verify door a second such call follows at `at: 1` for the destination, and it too is an ordinary
477	claim with no arrows in. There is no separate event for either, and the browser needs none: from this
478	side both are the same fact the rest of the run keeps repeating — *the map got bigger*.
479	
480	**NFR-7's wording is corrected here.** It reads *"streaming first-paint within 1s of the first
481	token"*, and this pipeline has no first token to be within a second of: the model boundary returns
482	**one whole proposal per call** (record 0006), and one proposal takes seconds to come back. A budget
483	measured from the first token would be a budget nothing could ever miss, because the thing it starts
484	timing from arrives at the same moment as the thing it times. So the budget is measured from the
485	request being accepted, and what has to be on screen within the second is a skeleton at its column —
486	which is the honest reading of what UX-8 promises anyway. The sentence `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md`
487	should carry instead is in this pull request's report; the requirement itself is not this chapter's
488	to edit.
489	
490	**There is no spinner anywhere in this product** — not here, not on the launchpad, not on the
491	`insert` route, not while a lazily fetched midpoint chip is in flight. Waiting is always shown as the
492	shape of the thing being waited for: a reserved rectangle where a claim will go, an absence with its
493	reason where a number will go. Checklist line 2 is the standing check and
494	`test_there_is_no_spinner_anywhere` is the automated one.
495	
496	### B2 — What a skeleton is, and what it never becomes
497	
498	A skeleton tile is **a reserved rectangle**. Not a shimmer, not a pulse, not a grey bar sliding
499	across a card.
500	
501	* **Its box is a tile's box.** 280 pixels wide (`TILE_WIDTH`), 152 tall (`TILE_MIN_HEIGHT`, the floor
502	  of the tile's own clamp), on the eight-pixel grid, with one border at `--hairline`. It is drawn on
503	  `--surface`, not on `--surface-raised`, so it reads as a space held open rather than as a card with
504	  nothing in it. **The border is dashed** — a solid hairline is what a claim's tile has, and a box
505	  the same weight as a tile beside a tile reads as a tile whose text has not loaded.
506	* **It carries two things and nothing else** *(amended 2026-09-21: this said "one line", and the code
507	  draws two)*. A mark reading **held open**, in the smallest type this product allows and no smaller,
508	  so that what the box is is readable rather than inferred — a reader meeting an empty dashed box for
509	  the first time has no way to know it is a promise rather than a fault. And one line: the first
510	  rectangle carries the reader's own sentence, every later one carries *one step on from "…"*,
511	  quoting the open claim it hangs off — so the reader can see not just that more is coming but *where
512	  from*. No chips, no dates, no clippings, no kind silhouette, no badge, and no number of any kind.
513	* **Its only movement is opacity, at most `--duration-fast`.** Nothing scales, pulses, sweeps or
514	  loops. An animated placeholder is a tool pretending to be busy; a held rectangle is a tool saying
515	  where the next thing goes.
516	* **It is not draggable**, like every other tile (INV-workbench.28).
517	
518	**Where skeletons come from — three events, and nothing else.**
519	
520	| Event | What it leaves on screen |
521	|---|---|
522	| `generation_started` | Exactly one skeleton, for the hypothesis, carrying the sentence as typed |
523	| `proposal_accepted` | One skeleton per claim named in `frontier`, each hanging off that claim. The set is **rebuilt**, so a claim that has left the frontier loses its rectangle in the same frame |
524	| `proposal_rejected` | The same, from the same field. A claim closed by its third refusal in a row is gone from `frontier` here, so its rectangle comes down on the refusal rather than waiting for an accepted proposal that may never come |
525	| `beliefs_propagated` | **Every skeleton goes.** The frontier is empty by definition once the map is finished, so there is nothing left for one to stand for |
526	| `failed` | **Every skeleton goes** *(added 2026-09-21)*. A rectangle is a promise that a claim is coming, and after a run breaks nothing is. The claims that were still open are in the working either way, so nothing is lost by taking the boxes down; what is lost by leaving them up is a reader waiting for a claim for ever |
527	| *the body ending with no terminator at all* | **Every skeleton goes** *(added 2026-09-21)*. The same rule, for the case that is not an event: see B3's *a stream that simply stops*, below |
528	
529	So the skeletons on screen are the **frontier, drawn** — rebuilt from whichever growth event arrived
530	last, and emptied when the world lands. That is a fact the stream states, never a guess the browser
531	makes, and it is the whole reason both growth events carry `frontier` rather than only the accepted
532	one.
533	
534	**Two things close a claim and neither makes an event of its own**: the model answering *Stop* on
535	that line, and its third refusal in a row. Both are recorded — a *Stop* leaves a transcript line, and
536	every refusal is already a `proposal_rejected` — and the browser is never *told* a claim closed,
537	because it can read it: the next growth event's `frontier` simply no longer names it. **So no
538	rectangle ever stands where nothing is coming**, and no event exists whose only job is to announce
539	that nothing happened.
540	
541	It is worth saying what the browser therefore *cannot* say. The stream has no "a call has gone out"
542	event, so **one skeleton stands for one claim still open, not for one model call in flight.** Three
543	calls may be out against one open claim and there is still one rectangle. If a later stack wants the
544	count of calls on screen, the stream has to say it; the browser must not count for itself. (Open
545	question 1.)
546	
547	**A skeleton is never a claim.** It has no identifier on the map — its name, `skeleton:<claim id>`,
548	names a rectangle. It never enters `WorldView.claims`, never reaches the network, never appears in
549	the outline view, cannot be selected, cannot open the Inspector, and has no belief chip to leave
550	empty. There is no number on it to be a number nobody computed, because there is no number on it at
551	all.
552	
553	**On Hormuz, three rectangles and then two.** Walking the run in B3's table: after step 3 — the
554	proposal that brings **B**, caused by **C**, with the single arrow `C → B` — the frontier names H, C
555	and B, so three rectangles stand at the growing edge, reading *one step on from "The Strait of Hormuz
556	is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*, *…from "Lloyd's war-risk
557	insurance premium for Gulf transits falls below 0.4%"* and *…from "Brent crude settles below $68 for
558	five sessions"*.
559	
560	**Step 4 takes one of them down, and it is an accepted proposal that does it.** That step adds the
561	arrow `H → B` and no claim at all; H now causes three claims, which is its full width, so H closes
562	and step 4's `frontier` names only C and B. H's rectangle goes on that event — not because anything
563	announced it, but because the frontier stopped naming it. **N1 never had one:** it arrived at step 2
564	as a `not_tradeable` ending, and an ending has nothing downstream of it, so it never joined the
565	frontier in the first place. The map is honest that the chain stops there, and it is honest about it
566	by drawing nothing rather than by drawing something that then disappears.
567	
568	### B3 — The whole run, as the canvas sees it
569	
570	The same generation `spec/generation/proposals.md` B4 writes out call by call, read from this side of
571	the wire. `at` is the transcript position; the last column is what stands at the growing edge **after**
572	that event has been folded in.
573	
574	| `at` | Event | What lands on the canvas | Rectangles standing |
575	|---|---|---|---|
576	| 0 | `proposal_accepted` | **H** — *"The Strait of Hormuz is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*. `links` is empty; the first rectangle becomes this tile | H |
577	| 1 | `proposal_accepted` | **C** and the wire `H → C` | H · C |
578	| 2 | `proposal_accepted` | **N1** and the wire `H → N1`. An ending, so it never joins the frontier and never gets a rectangle | H · C |
579	| 3 | `proposal_accepted` | **B** and the wire `C → B` — one claim, one incoming arrow | H · C · B |
580	| 4 | `proposal_accepted` | **No claim at all**: `proposition` is null and `links` holds the one new wire `H → B`. H reaches its full width here and closes | C · B |
581	| 5 | `proposal_accepted` | **M1** and the wire `B → M1`. A tradeable ending | C · B |
582	| 6 | `proposal_rejected` | Nothing on the canvas; one row on the refusal strip (B5). The frontier is unchanged — this is B's first refusal, not its third | C · B |
583	| 7 | `proposal_accepted` | **M2** and the wire `B → M2`. A tradeable ending | C · B |
584	| — | nothing on the wire | C answers *Stop*; a transcript line and no event | B |
585	| — | nothing on the wire | B answers *Stop*; the last open claim closes | — |
586	| — | `beliefs_propagated` | Every chip fills, at once (B4). Every rectangle goes | — |
587	| — | `receipt` · `done` | The receipt strip; the stop reason, `reached_terminal`, because the last open claim answered *Stop* (B7). `claims=6`, `links=6`, `rejected=1` — count them off the rows above | — |
588	
589	Two things worth reading off that table. **The transcript's numbering has gaps** — a client sees 7
590	and then the closing events, and the two missing positions are the two stops, which make no event
591	because nothing about the map changed. And **no event ever says a claim closed**: the rectangle for H
592	comes down at step 4 because step 4's `frontier` stopped naming it, and the last two come down on
593	`beliefs_propagated`, where the frontier is empty by definition.
594	
595	The map that grows is **not the shipped fixture and does not pretend to be**: six claims where the
596	fixture has seven, and no feedback arrow `B → R`, because a proposal has no `reflexive` field and
597	nothing can propose one. Every chapter in this part works the fixture; this one works the run, and
598	the difference is a fact about generation rather than a discrepancy to smooth over.
599	
600	**Where a claim lands is decided by its causes, not by when it arrived.** The layout is the layered
601	one [`layout-and-zoom.md`](layout-and-zoom.md) owns: a claim sits in a column to the right of
602	everything that causes it. N1 arrives third and lands in column 1; B arrives fourth and lands in
603	column 2. The picture reads causality, and arrival order leaves no trace in it.
604	
605	**Nothing that is already on screen moves.** This is not new machinery and growth adds none. The
606	rule already lives in `readPositions` in `frontend/src/graph/elkGraph.ts`, in those words: *a tile
607	that had a position keeps that position, to the pixel, and only a tile that had none takes a new
608	one.* Growth is the case that rule was written for. Every claim the engine sends is strictly
609	downstream of the map so far — a `ClaimProposal` brings one claim and the one arrow into it, so that
610	arrow's source is always a claim that already exists — which is exactly the precondition
611	INV-workbench.22 names. A late arrival finds a gap; nothing above it, beside it or before it shifts.
612	
613	**A wire draws only after both of its ends exist.** In practice the engine makes this true by
614	construction, twice over: a `ClaimProposal` brings the claim and the arrow into it in one event, and
615	an arrows-only proposal names two claims that are already on the map. The reducer does not rely on
616	either. An arrow whose two ends are not both on the map goes into `waitingWires` and is drawn the
617	moment the second end arrives. The list is expected to stay empty for ever, and the test that proves
618	the rule **builds** a stream that fills it rather than assuming one cannot exist. A wire with one end
619	nowhere is a picture of something that is not true, and half a wire is worse than no wire.
620	
621	**The wave is the one already budgeted.** Each wire arrives with the propagation wave
622	[`color-motion-type.md`](color-motion-type.md) spends: about 200 milliseconds (`--duration-wave`),
623	its column 60 milliseconds (`--duration-stagger`) after the column before. It is already built —
624	`.canvas[data-arriving="yes"]` in `frontend/src/graph/canvas.css`, with a `wave-<n>` class per
625	column. Growth switches it on per arrival instead of once per map, and adds no fourth animation to
626	the budget of three.
627	
628	**The honest wart, and the one event that could cause it.** An arrows-only proposal — step 4 above —
629	joins two tiles that are already placed, and because the pin is absolute the wire is drawn where they
630	sit rather than re-laying out the map to suit it. On this run that costs nothing: H is in column 0
631	and B in column 2, so `H → B` points rightwards like every other wire and no column would have moved
632	anyway. But an arrows-only proposal whose source happens to sit *right* of its target would be drawn
633	pointing backwards, which is honest about where the tiles are and misleading about the argument. The
634	trade is the one [`layout-and-zoom.md`](layout-and-zoom.md) anti-pattern 7 makes: the map should be
635	still while you read it, and losing your place is the worse failure. Whether the map re-lays out once
636	when the run finishes is Open question 2, **answered below**.
637	
638	**A stream that simply stops** *(added 2026-09-21)*. Every stream a reader stayed for ends in exactly
639	one `done` or one `failed`. A body that ends with neither is a dropped connection —
640	[`spec/generation/streaming.md`](../generation/streaming.md): *"a dropped stream is a finished
641	generation with no terminator. The browser says the stream ended early and offers to run it again."*
642	A server restarted, a proxy gave up on a connection it thought was idle, a laptop slept during a
643	ten-minute run: none of those is a fault anybody on this side can name, and none is a `failed` event,
644	because none of them is the run saying anything at all.
645	
646	What the browser does is three things and no more. **The rectangles come down**, which is the other
647	half of *no rectangle ever stands where nothing is coming* — after this, nothing is, and a map left
648	growing for ever is the one screen in this product that lies without saying a word: it is drawn
649	exactly as a map about to change and it is never going to change again. **The map is kept**, every
650	claim and arrow that arrived, with nothing invented to fill the gap and nothing greyed. And **one
651	plain sentence**, in the same line under the map that says why any other run ended, with **the offer
652	to run the same sentence again beside it** — an offer that says on its face what pressing it costs:
653	*run it again — this asks the model again, and spends again* on a copy with a key, and *play it again
654	— this plays the recording again, and spends nothing* on one without. A control that quietly spends
655	money the second time it is pressed is the one control in this product that must say so before it is
656	pressed.
657	
658	It is not folded from an event, because there is no event: the reader of the stream is the only thing
659	that can notice a body ending, and it hands the reducer that fact by name (`theStreamEnded`) rather
660	than by inventing a ninth event the server never sent. The working as far as it got is still readable
661	at `GET /api/generate/{generation_id}/transcript`, which is the whole reason this state keeps the map
662	rather than clearing it.
663	
664	### B4 — Chips resolve last, and they resolve once
665	
666	**While the map grows, every model chip reads *no engine yet*.** The claims that arrive carry their
667	stated `prior`, and the tile never draws a prior — a second number beside the model's would be a
668	fourth voice ([`tiles-ports-wires.md`](tiles-ports-wires.md)). So a growing map is the same picture
669	this part already ships: real claims, real arrows, real provenance marks, and an absence with its
670	reason in every likelihood slot.
671	
672	**When `beliefs_propagated` arrives, they all fill at once.** One event, one world, every number.
673	The chip's own sentence switches from the *stated* pair to record 0014's *computed* pair with no
674	change to the component, because `WorldView.versions` arrives on the same world and that is the one
675	field the chip reads to choose (Kent, K3; `tiles-ports-wires.md`, *What the model chip says about its
676	own range*).
677	
678	**Never per tile, and never twice.** A likelihood that changed four times as its causes arrived would
679	be four numbers nobody computed: the first three would each be the answer to a question about a map
680	that no longer exists. There is exactly one propagation per generation and exactly one
681	`beliefs_propagated` event, so a chip goes from its absence to its number once and stays.
682	
683	**The reveal is not the number-roll.** The third budgeted animation rolls a likelihood from an old
684	figure to a new one, and here there is no old figure — there is an absence. So the chips appear with
685	an opacity change at `--duration-fast` and nothing rolls. The number-roll still has nothing to roll
686	until an edit moves a number, which is this stack's second pull request.
687	
688	### B5 — Every refusal is on screen, in the validator's own words
689	
690	**A rejected proposal is an event, not an error.** Nothing is retried quietly out of sight and
691	nothing is swallowed. The engine may try again — up to three fresh proposals for one open claim,
692	none of them told why the last was refused (Kent, G4; record 0003's dated amendment) — and **every
693	one of those attempts that was refused is on screen.**
694	
695	The refusal strip is one row per refusal, in the order they happened, newest last. A row carries the
696	model's own words on its first line, ellipsized at a word boundary, and beneath them the validator's
697	own sentence — **one per rule broken**, because a proposal that broke three rules and shows one is a
698	refusal the reader has half seen. The rows are short and there are few of them; a run with a strip
699	long enough to need trimming has a prompt problem, not a layout problem.
700	
701	Two rules the strip obeys, both inherited rather than invented. **The sentence is the validator's, as
702	it wrote it** — `spec/graph/validity.md` owns that copy, and its rules for it are that a message
703	names the claim by its words, never by its identifier, and says what is missing rather than that
704	something failed. The browser never composes a sentence about a refusal. And **a refused claim is
705	never drawn as a tile and never given an identifier** — `claim_in_words` is quoted and nothing else
706	is done with it, which is the same rule as B2's.
707	
708	**On Hormuz, at step 6.** Every recording must hold at least one refusal (record 0012), and the map's
709	own shape supplies it. Expanding B, the model proposes an arrow rather than a claim — `B → H`,
710	*cheaper crude reduces the incentive to close the strait*. Read on its own it is a reasonable
711	sentence; added to the map it closes `H → B → H`, because step 4 has already drawn `H → B`. The rules
712	refuse it with exactly one violation, and its message is the validator's, word for word:
713	
714	```
715	proposal 6   refused
716	   "cheaper crude reduces the incentive to close the strait"
717	   These claims form a loop with no delay in it: "The Strait of Hormuz is open to
718	   unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days" → "Brent crude settles
719	   below $68 for five sessions" → "The Strait of Hormuz is open to unrestricted
720	   commercial transit for 14 consecutive days". Mark the arrow where a market feeds
721	   back on the world as reflexive and give it a delay, or remove one arrow.
722	```
723	
724	Nothing moves on the canvas when that row appears. B is on its **first** refusal, not its third, so
725	step 6's `frontier` still names C and B and both rectangles stay exactly where they were. Step 7 is
726	the same call asked again with a byte-identical prompt — the next call is never told what was wrong
727	— and it comes back with M2.
728	
729	That row is half the product. It is the moment a reader can see that our own code, not the model,
730	decides what the map is allowed to contain — and it says the one thing that would have made the
731	arrow legal, which is the difference between a rejection and an insult.
732	
733	`proposal 6` is `at`, the engine's own position in the transcript, printed so the row can be found
734	again in the Inspector. Selecting the row opens the Inspector's **this generation** section at that
735	line.
736	
737	### B6 — The receipt strip, and where a transcript is read
738	
739	**This answers [`inspector.md`](inspector.md) open question 2.**
740	
741	When `receipt` arrives, the strip beneath the refusals fills in. It prints what the engine sent and
742	adds nothing up:
743	
744	```
745	THIS GENERATION
746	  model            <Receipt.model>
747	  calls            <Receipt.calls>
748	  tokens in        <Receipt.input_tokens>
749	  tokens out       <Receipt.output_tokens>
750	  read from cache  <Receipt.cache_read_tokens>
751	  web searches     <Receipt.searches>
752	  cost             <Receipt.dollars>, in the two places money has
753	  took             <Receipt.seconds> — "the replay took", on a replay
754	  how hard the
755	    model tried    <Receipt.effort>
756	  mode             live
757	```
758	
759	**Money has two places** *(coordinator, 2026-09-21)*. It printed up to four — `$0.6132` — which is
760	the same fake precision checklist line 4 exists to stop, in the place a reader is most likely to
761	compare two runs: the fourth place is a rounding of a price table, and four places read as a
762	measurement. **And a guard word exactly when it is true** (K2): a run that spent nothing prints
763	`$0.00`, which is a computed zero and reads as one, and a run that spent something and less than a
764	cent prints `<$0.01`, because `$0.00` there would say a run was free when it was not. One function,
765	used by the generation's strip and the insert's alike, so the two cannot come to write a cost two
766	ways.
767	
768	**And `took` says whose clock it is.** On a live run it is how long the run took. On a replay it is
769	how long the **replay** took — a few seconds of paced playback beside a map that took eleven minutes
770	to make — so the row reads *the replay took*. A reader comparing the two figures without that word
771	would conclude this product is two hundred times faster than it is. The recorded run's own duration
772	is not on the wire; when it is, this row can carry it and say which is which.
773	
774	**Amended 2026-09-21 — there are ten readings, and the tenth is how hard the model tried.** A plain
775	word: `default` when nothing was asked for and the service's own applied, otherwise `low`, `medium`,
776	`high`, `xhigh` or `max`. One setting with two pinned defaults behind it — **a recording is made rich
777	and a live run is made fast** (Kent, G13) — so two maps of the same sentence at the same seed can
778	differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the sentence, and a reader comparing one with the
779	other is entitled to see which they are looking at. It is the word the service takes rather than a
780	number, because a number would be this browser translating one thing into another and printing the
781	translation.
782	
783	Four things about it.
784	
785	* **Every one of those is a field.** The browser does not add the two token counts together, does not
786	  work out a cost from a token count and a price, and does not time anything itself. A price table
787	  lives in exactly one module on the server (`engine/pricing.py`) with the day it was read beside it,
788	  and the dollars on this strip came from there. **Searches are a row of their own** because they are
789	  billed apart from tokens: without that row, `dollars` is a number a reader could check against the
790	  token counts and find wrong.
791	* **Checklist line 4 is about likelihoods.** *"No number shows more than two significant figures, and
792	  none is missing its range"* is the rule that stops a fake-precise `.347` reaching the screen
793	  (NFR-1). A token count, a call count, a duration and a dollar figure are counts and measurements:
794	  they are printed whole, in `--font-mono` with fixed-width digits, and they have no range because
795	  nothing sampled them. The same reading already lets a lag chip say *14 days* and a tile be 280
796	  pixels wide.
797	* **In replay the mode reads `replay`**, the recording's date sits beside it, and `cost` reads what
798	  the rebuilt receipt carries, which is zero. That zero is a computed zero — the recording was played,
799	  nothing was called, so nothing was spent — not an empty slot, and it is printed rather than hidden.
800	* **Before the receipt arrives the strip is not there.** No running estimate, no ticking cost, no
801	  progress bar. A cost nobody has totalled is a number nobody computed.
802	
803	**The working lives in the Inspector, and it is the panel's third subject.** Until now the Inspector
804	opened on a claim or an arrow. It now also opens on the generation itself, and that section holds
805	*(amended 2026-09-21)*: the seed the run drew with and the prompt's fingerprint, whole, each with the
806	sentence saying what it is for; the whole transcript, one line per proposal in order, accepted or
807	refused, each accepted one naming the claim it became and each refused one carrying every sentence
808	the validator wrote; a line per event name this build did not know, with how many of each arrived;
809	and one sentence pointing at the strip for what the run cost. **It carries no copy of the receipt's
810	ten readings.** It is drawn from the moment there is a generation, with whatever has arrived in it
811	and an em dash in each slot that has not — a section that appeared only once everything had landed
812	would be a panel that is empty exactly while a reader is most likely to open it. The transcript is
813	read from `GET /api/generate/{generation_id}/transcript`, which the server holds
814	in memory for the life of the process — there is no storage in this stack, and a transcript outliving
815	the process is stack 05's question (FR-31).
816	
817	**An event this build does not know is ignored, and said out loud.** The reader folds it in as a name
818	and a count and changes nothing else: it does not throw, because a browser that crashes on a new
819	event makes the server unable to add one; and it does not disappear, because a dropped event makes a
820	missing feature look like a working one. The line is the only place it shows, and one line in the
821	transcript is the right size for *"this build saw two events it has no name for"*.
822	
823	Every number on the strip is therefore one click from its why in the strictest sense
824	[`inspector.md`](inspector.md) INV-workbench.51 asks for: the click opens the panel at the transcript
825	that produced the count.
826	
827	### B7 — The Verify door: a graded path, or an honest *no path reaches this*
828	
829	The Verify door is **one extra field on the same input bar**, not a second screen: the reader names
830	where they think it ends. On Hormuz: *the Polymarket contract "Brent below $70 on 2026-10-31"*. The
831	generation runs exactly as before, and one more event arrives.
832	
833	**`kind: "reached"` — the graded path.** A card at the top of the dock, naming the steps of
834	`Verdict.path` in order in the claims' own words, with the multiplied-out likelihood of those steps
835	beside it (INV-8), the number taken from `Verdict.product` and multiplied by nobody here. Under it,
836	word for word, the same wart the Inspector's path bar prints, because there is one wording and one
837	place it is written ([`inspector.md`](inspector.md) B5): the factors are each read on their own
838	resolve-by day, so the product multiplies numbers read on different days, and **it is not a joint
839	probability**. The card and the path bar share the sentence, not the component *(corrected
840	2026-09-21)*: one exported constant, `PATH_PRODUCT_WART`, which the card prints and the bar prints.
841	They are two different components — the bar is a claim's own route with its chips, the card is the
842	Verify door's answer with its steps and its control — and saying they are one would have somebody
843	look for a shared component that does not exist. What must not drift is the wording, and a constant
844	is what stops wording drifting.
845	
846	**How long the route is is printed, never counted** *(added 2026-09-21)*. `Verdict.why` is the
847	engine's own sentence and it already says it — *"…reaches it in 2 steps"*. The card used to say it
848	again underneath, worked out as one fewer than the claims on `Verdict.path`: two derivations of one
849	fact, agreeing exactly until the day the engine counts a step differently, and then the card
850	contradicts itself in two adjacent paragraphs with nothing on screen to say which is right.
851	
852	**`kind: "no_path"` — a finding, drawn as a finding.** This is not a failure state and it does not
853	look like one. The card carries `Verdict.why` — the engine's own plain sentence — and names
854	`Verdict.nearest`, the closest claim the map did reach, with one control that selects that claim on
855	the map so the reader can see where the path stopped.
856	
857	**No bridge is drawn. Ever.** No dotted arrow from the nearest claim to the destination, no ghost
858	tile for the destination, no "probably connects" wording. A path that does not exist is the most
859	valuable thing this door can tell you, and drawing a faint one would be the traceability veto with a
860	dashed stroke.
861	
862	**`no_path` is on the verdict and nowhere else.** `Done.reason` has seven values and none of them is
863	`no_path`; it says why the *generation* stopped, which is a different question with a different
864	answer. A run can reach its claim cap and still have found a path, and a run can end cleanly and
865	have found none.
866	
867	**And when the generation itself stops, the strip says why, in the engine's words for it.** One
868	reason arrives, never a list, and it names **what closed the last claim that was still open** — with
869	the spending limit and the no-ending case overriding everything above them. `spec/generation/proposals.md`
870	B4 owns that rule; this table owns the words.
871	
872	| `Done.reason` | What the strip says |
873	|---|---|
874	| `reached_terminal` | The last line closed properly: it reached something you could trade, or a stated reason there is nothing to trade, or the model had nothing more to add. |
875	| `depth_cap` | The last line still open ran as far from your sentence as one generation goes, and stopped there. |
876	| `width_cap` | The last line still open was closed because that claim already has every effect one generation draws from it. |
877	| `claim_cap` | The last line still open was closed because the map was full. |
878	| `spend_cap` | The run reached its spending limit and stopped where it was. The receipt says what it spent. |
879	| `refusal_cap` | One line was abandoned: three proposals in a row for it were refused. |
880	| `no_terminal` | One last call asked every open claim where it ends, and none of them ends in something you could trade. |
881	
882	Two things those seven sentences do on purpose. **No sentence blames the model for our own rules.**
883	Three refusals in a row is our validator turning proposals down and our cap deciding that three is
884	enough; a sentence reading *"the model stopped answering"* would be a screen accusing a third party
885	of a decision we took, which is the reverse of the receipt this product writes everywhere else. And
886	**each one names the cap and not its value**, because the stream carries no value. A limit the browser
887	printed from memory would be a number nobody on this screen computed, and a limit that had quietly
888	changed on the server would then be a number that was wrong. The values and their justifications are
889	`spec/generation/proposals.md`'s.
890	
891	**`failed` is the eighth thing that can happen, and it is not one of the seven.** The map that had
892	been built stays exactly where it is — nothing is cleared, nothing is greyed — and one line appears
893	under it carrying `Failed.message`, which is one plain sentence and never a stack trace. A reader
894	whose run broke after twenty claims keeps the twenty claims.
895	
896	### B8 — The input bar, and **Add a claim**
897	
898	**Three fields, one button, and no more** (FR-1, FR-2).
899	
900	1. **The sentence.** One line, the hypothesis, in the reader's own words.
901	2. **Where it ends**, optional. The Verify door. One field, hinted with what it is for.
902	3. **Your own likelihood.** A range with an explicit **I don't know** state (FR-2). Three handles on
903	   one track — the number and the two ends of its range — spelled beside the track in exactly the
904	   one-line form the chip uses, `.55 (.40–.70)`, under the same two-significant-figure rule and the
905	   same certainty guard ([`keyboard-and-access.md`](keyboard-and-access.md) B6), so the control
906	   cannot post a `1.0`.
907	
908	**The button is `Build the map`**, word for word, and it is the same button on both doors. Not
909	*Generate*, which is the pipeline's word rather than the reader's, and not *Explore* or *Verify*,
910	which are the two doors and are already named by whether the second field has anything in it — a
911	button whose label changed as the reader typed would be a control that moved under them. It is
912	written once, beside the six operation buttons, in the Interface words table in
913	[`../vocabulary.md`](../vocabulary.md); this chapter copies it and never paraphrases it.
914	
915	**"I don't know" is a state of the control, not a value.** It is where the control starts, and while
916	it holds, the request carries **no** `user_belief` at all — not a `.5`, not a wide band, not a null
917	that something downstream treats as a half. A reader who has not said what they think has not said
918	what they think, and a tool that fills that in for them has invented the one number it had no
919	business inventing.
920	
921	**The reader's number is stored as a `user` belief on the hypothesis and is never overwritten.** The
922	model's belief and the reader's are two slots that are never merged (INV-11), and a generation
923	writes the model's.
924	
925	**With no model key, the bar is visibly disabled and says why** — record 0012's sentence, the same
926	one the launchpad carries, word for word. Never silently inert: a field that takes typing and then
927	does nothing reads as a broken tool, where a field that says why reads as an unfinished one, and only
928	one of those is true.
929	
930	**Add a claim** — *"…but this also happens"* — is the one intervention that calls the model (PRD §10
931	anti-pattern 2's single exception: re-prompt only for an insert, and only over the affected subtree).
932	It posts to `POST /api/generate/insert` — `{base_id, branch, claim_in_words}` — and gets back **one**

content.content:
1	/**
2	 * A map drawing itself, in a real browser, against a real server, **with no
3	 * model key at all**.
4	 *
5	 * It is the one thing no component test can claim: that a reviewer who has
6	 * configured nothing can open the first screen, press a card, and watch a map
7	 * build itself claim by claim — with a reserved rectangle standing where the next
8	 * claim will go, every proposal the rules refused on screen in the validator's
9	 * own words, and a receipt at the end saying what it cost.
10	 *
11	 * **It plays a recording, through the same route, the same eight events and the
12	 * same canvas a live run uses.** The only substitution anywhere is where the
13	 * bytes came from, which is what makes this evidence about the live route rather
14	 * than about a second one.
15	 *
16	 * **It skips itself when there is nothing recorded**, in one line saying so. The
17	 * recordings are made against a real key by the person who holds it; until one is
18	 * committed under `backend/recordings/`, this test has nothing to play and says
19	 * that rather than failing. The moment one lands it runs, with no change here.
20	 *
21	 * **Nothing below reads a value the screen has not settled on.** The waiting is
22	 * `waiting.ts`'s, the same helpers the stored example's test uses: a named signal
23	 * every time, never a sleep, and never `innerText` — which is empty until the
24	 * drawing library has measured a tile, and which is how a chip that plainly read
25	 * `.19` was once read as nothing at all.
26	 *
27	 * **A growing map needs one signal the stored one does not**, and it is the
28	 * reason this file has helpers of its own: on a stored map everything arrives at
29	 * once, and here the screen is *correct* and *incomplete* at the same moment for
30	 * minutes at a time. So every read below waits for the count it is about — this
31	 * many claims, this many rectangles, the receipt — rather than for the page.
32	 *
33	 * Nothing here is a number typed into this file. Every figure is read off the
34	 * screen and compared with itself across a change, or checked for its shape.
35	 */
36	
37	import { expect, type Page, test } from "@playwright/test";
38	import { whereTheMapCameToRest, whereTheTileSits } from "./waiting.js";
39	
40	/** The sentence the first screen's first card carries, as a reader would type it. */
41	const THE_SENTENCE = "The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week.";
42	
43	/**
44	 * How long a whole run is allowed to take before this test gives up on it.
45	 *
46	 * **A replay takes as long as its recording**, because the pacing is the
47	 * server's and the number of events is the file's — a twenty-proposal run is
48	 * four times the twenty seconds a five-proposal one takes, and neither number
49	 * is this test's to know. So the bound below is not a measurement and is not
50	 * tuned to a machine: it is generous on purpose, and exists only so that a run
51	 * which has genuinely stopped fails as a test rather than hanging.
52	 *
53	 * The default fifteen seconds is the wrong bound for exactly one thing in this
54	 * file — waiting for a run to finish — and the right one everywhere else, so it
55	 * is named here and used there.
56	 */
57	const A_WHOLE_RUN = 120_000;

59	// Every test here plays a recording from beginning to end, so each needs room
60	// for one. It is set on the file rather than in the configuration because it is
61	// a fact about these tests: the stored example's tests next door are right to
62	// be held to a minute.
63	test.describe.configure({ timeout: A_WHOLE_RUN + 60_000 });

65	/**
66	 * What this copy of the server says it can play back without a key.

69	 * anything to do at all is a fact about the server, and reading it off the page
70	 * would make the skip depend on the very screen being tested.

72	async function whatCanBeReplayed(page: Page): Promise<{ example: string }[]> {
73	  const answer = await page.request.get("/api/readyz");
74	  const said = (await answer.json()) as { replayable?: { example: string }[] };

78	/** What watching a whole run saw. */
79	interface WhatItSaw {
80	  /** True when, at some moment, a rectangle stood and not one claim had arrived. */
81	  readonly rectangleBeforeAnyClaim: boolean;
82	  /**
83	   * The words on the first rectangle, read at a moment when no claim had
84	   * arrived — so it is the one held open for the reader's own sentence and not
85	   * one of the frontier's, which carry *one step on from "…"*.
86	   *
87	   * Empty when no such moment was seen.
88	   */
89	  readonly firstRectangleSaid: string;
90	  /** The most rectangles that stood at once. */
91	  readonly mostRectangles: number;
92	  /**
93	   * True when, at some moment, two boxes on the map stood in the same place.
94	   *
95	   * The place they would share is the map's origin, where the hypothesis is:
96	   * a box the layout has not placed yet used to be drawn there, so every
97	   * arriving claim sat on top of the first one until the layout answered.
98	   */
99	  readonly everStacked: boolean;
100	  /**
101	   * How many rectangles stood at the moment each claim arrived, in order.
102	   *
103	   * The growing edge saying where the map is going, step by step, rather than
104	   * only at the start. **The last entry is allowed to be none**: the frontier
105	   * empties when the last claim closes, and no rectangle may stand where
106	   * nothing is coming.
107	   */
108	  readonly heldWhenEachClaimArrived: readonly number[];
109	  /**
110	   * How many claims were on the map, every time that number changed.
111	   *
112	   * The sequence rather than the largest of them: the largest is whatever the
113	   * map ended up with, which is a fact about the end and says nothing at all
114	   * about how the map got there. A map that appeared all at once and a map that
115	   * grew claim by claim have the same largest number and completely different
116	   * sequences.
117	   */
118	  readonly claimsWentOn: readonly number[];
119	  /**
120	   * How many claims were on the map the first time any likelihood appeared, and
121	   * how many appeared at that moment.
122	   *
123	   * Both are zero when none ever did. Together they are the statement that the
124	   * chips resolve **last** and **once**: the first number arrives when the map
125	   * is complete, and every other number arrives in the same breath.
126	   */
127	  readonly whenTheNumbersCame: { readonly claims: number; readonly numbers: number };
128	}

130	/** Where the page keeps what it has seen of itself. */
131	declare global {
132	  interface Window {
133	    theRecord?: WhatItSaw & { rectangleBeforeAnyClaim: boolean };
134	    stopWatching?: () => void;
135	  }
136	}

138	/**
139	 * Have the page start watching itself, before anything is asked for.
140	 *
141	 * **Four of the things this test is for are about a screen that is moving**, and
142	 * a moving screen cannot be checked by looking at it once: *a rectangle is drawn
143	 * before any claim*, *rectangles stand at the growing edge*, *the claims arrive
144	 * one at a time* and *not one likelihood is on screen until the map is finished*
145	 * are each true at some moments and false at others, and by the time an
146	 * assertion has been written the moment it was about is gone. Polling for one of
147	 * them races the run; asserting after it is over asserts about the wrong moment.
148	 *
149	 * So the page watches itself. Every change to the page is looked at — which is
150	 * every moment the screen was different — and what was on it is written down.
151	 * Nothing here sleeps, and nothing here can miss a moment that a poll would have
152	 * stepped over.
153	 *
154	 * **It is installed before the press**, and awaited, so that the very first
155	 * frame of the run is inside the record. Starting it after the press leaves the
156	 * one moment the first assertion is about — a rectangle standing with no claim
157	 * beside it — outside the window being watched, on a fast replay.
158	 *
159	 * @param page The page the map will be on.
160	 */
161	async function startWatching(page: Page): Promise<void> {
162	  await page.evaluate(() => {
163	    const record = {
164	      rectangleBeforeAnyClaim: false,
165	      firstRectangleSaid: "",
166	      mostRectangles: 0,
167	      everStacked: false,
168	      heldWhenEachClaimArrived: [] as number[],
169	      claimsWentOn: [] as number[],
170	      whenTheNumbersCame: { claims: 0, numbers: 0 },
171	    };
172	    window.theRecord = record;
173	
174	    const look = (): void => {
175	      const held = document.querySelectorAll(".skeleton-tile").length;
176	      const claims = document.querySelectorAll(".tile").length;
177	      // A chip says on its own face whether it is showing a number or words,
178	      // and that is the marker to count: every chip renders a reading, and on
179	      // a growing map most of them are reading an absence out.
180	      const numbers = document.querySelectorAll('.belief-chip[data-reading="number"]').length;
181	
182	      if (held > 0 && claims === 0) {
183	        record.rectangleBeforeAnyClaim = true;
184	        // **Read here, and never again from the live page.** What the first
185	        // rectangle says is true of one moment: the moment after it is drawn
186	        // and before the first claim replaces it with the frontier's. Reading
187	        // it in a second round trip asks a screen that has moved on — and on a
188	        // cold machine the whole run can finish in between, so the rectangle is
189	        // not merely different, it is gone.
190	        record.firstRectangleSaid = document.querySelector(".skeleton-tile")?.textContent ?? "";
191	      }
192	      record.mostRectangles = Math.max(record.mostRectangles, held);
193	      if (record.claimsWentOn[record.claimsWentOn.length - 1] !== claims) {
194	        // What the growing edge was saying at the moment this claim arrived.
195	        if (claims > 0) {
196	          record.heldWhenEachClaimArrived.push(held);
197	        }
198	        record.claimsWentOn.push(claims);
199	      }
200	      // Two boxes in one place. The place they would share is the map's origin,
201	      // where a box the layout has not placed yet used to be drawn.
202	      const places = [...document.querySelectorAll(".react-flow__node")].map(
203	        (one) => (one as HTMLElement).style.transform,
204	      );
205	      if (new Set(places).size !== places.length) {
206	        record.everStacked = true;
207	      }
208	      if (numbers > 0 && record.whenTheNumbersCame.numbers === 0) {
209	        record.whenTheNumbersCame = { claims, numbers };
210	      }
211	    };
212	
213	    const watching = new MutationObserver(look);
214	    window.stopWatching = () => watching.disconnect();
215	    watching.observe(document.body, { subtree: true, childList: true, attributes: true });
216	    look();
217	  });
218	}

2	 * Turning a world into the tiles and wires the canvas draws.

9	import type { Node } from "@xyflow/react";
10	import type { ClaimView, WorldView } from "../world";
11	import { NOT_ON_THIS_MAP } from "../world/naming";
12	import type { LayoutEdge, LayoutTile } from "./elkGraph";
